Henry VIII. King of England from 1509 to 1547, he is best known for initiating the English Reformation and separating the Church of England from papal authority. He married six times in his desperate quest for a male heir. These marriages, which can be summarized as divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived, transformed England's religious landscape and centralized royal power like never before.

The Act of Supremacy in 1534 declared Henry the Supreme Head of the Church of England, establishing his ecclesiastical authority. What followed was the Dissolution of the Monasteries, a campaign that saw him dissolve and confiscate the wealth of Catholic monasteries throughout England, Wales, and Ireland. Before his split with Rome, Henry had actually been granted the title Fidei Defensor, Defender of the Faith, by Pope Leo X in 1521, a title English monarchs still bear despite his later break with papal authority.

His chief minister Thomas Cromwell helped engineer the annulment of his first marriage to Catherine of Aragon, but fell out of favor and was later executed by the king. His daughter Elizabeth, born to Anne Boleyn, would rule during England's golden age. Though Henry had other children, it was Elizabeth who would become his most celebrated heir, bringing the final flourish to the Tudor dynasty that his obsessive quest for male heirs had nearly broken.
